dialogue:
ALEX: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.
JAMIE: Picture this. You are coordinating a group picnic. You send one message asking people to claim items. Within forty-eight hours you have seventeen replies, two people have claimed drinks, nobody has claimed plates, and someone has written, and I quote, "I'll just bring something."
RUFUS: That person is chaos in human form.
JAMIE: That person is every group chat, Rufus. The tool is Claude Artifacts. Anthropic documents that Claude can generate self-contained outputs, including formatted documents, code snippets, and small interactive files, directly inside a conversation. This is a hypothetical workflow. No hands-on result, no measured outcome, no actual picnic was saved.
ALEX: Right, so walk us through what the proposed workflow actually looks like.
JAMIE: You give Claude synthetic names and fictional items. Nothing real, no connected apps, no invitations sent. You ask it to draft a small assignment checklist as an artifact. The proposed output returns formatted assignments, an unassigned-items column, and a duplicate-item warning.
RUFUS: A warning. For the person who brings two desserts and acts surprised.
JAMIE: Exactly that person. And then you manually check every assignment yourself. Deliberately put a duplicate in and watch whether the warning catches it. That is the whole test.
ALEX: I want to push on the evidence here, because a proposed workflow and a vendor-documented capability are not a customer result.
JAMIE: Completely correct, and I will not dress it up. No measured time saving, no real implementation, no outcome to report. Anthropic documents this capability. The logic Claude generates can be wrong. You inspect the output yourself before it gets anywhere near a real group or a real event.
RUFUS: So the unassigned plates are still your problem.
JAMIE: Entirely your problem. The artifact makes the gap visible. Closing it is on the humans doing the reviewing.
RUFUS: Jamie, you are extremely worked up about a checklist for a fictional picnic.
JAMIE: Rufus, you once described a spreadsheet as "pretty much fine" and then three people ordered the same catering item for a team lunch.
RUFUS: That was a supply chain issue.
ALEX: It really wasn't.
JAMIE: I am just saying the problem is not fictional for everyone in this room.
RUFUS: Moving on.
JAMIE: One real limitation before anyone opens Claude. Artifacts need code execution enabled in your account. That is not a default everywhere. Check your settings first, because assuming it is available and finding it isn't is its own coordination failure.
ALEX: So what does someone do right now?
JAMIE: Open Claude. Invent five names. Assign fictional items. Ask for a small assignment checklist as an artifact. Then manually add a duplicate and read the output line by line before you trust any of it. Keep everything synthetic. The coordination still belongs to the people.
JAMIE: The artifact just surfaces the gaps before someone arrives holding the third bag of crisps nobody requested.
RUFUS: Low stakes, concrete, honest about what it cannot do.
JAMIE: That is the standard.
RUFUS: I'll try it. And I'll confirm who has the plates this time.
JAMIE: Write that down. And maybe the forks.
